name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER15_Q01 - Biodiversity levels IUCN records and insect richness

questiontext.text:
Read the following five statements regarding biodiversity and its components, and select the option containing only the correct statements:

(I) The term 'biodiversity' was popularised by the sociobiologist Edward Wilson to describe combined diversity at all levels of biological organisation.
(II) The Western Ghats have a greater amphibian species diversity than the Eastern Ghats, illustrating species diversity.
(III) India has greater ecosystem diversity than a Scandinavian country like Norway due to its deserts, rain forests, mangroves, coral reefs, wetlands, estuaries, and alpine meadows.
(IV) According to the IUCN (2004), the total number of plant and animal species described so far on earth is slightly more than 7 million.
(V) Among animals, insects are the most species-rich taxonomic group, making up more than 70 per cent of the total animal species.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Biodiversity encompasses genetic, species, and ecological levels of biological organisation, and global species inventories distinguish between described species and extrapolated total estimates.

Step 2: Evaluation of Edward Wilson, Species Diversity, and Ecosystem Diversity
Sociobiologist Edward Wilson popularised the term 'biodiversity' for combined diversity across all levels of biological organisation, from macromolecules within cells to biomes. The greater amphibian species richness in the Western Ghats compared to the Eastern Ghats exemplifies species diversity, while India's wide range of ecosystems (deserts, rain forests, mangroves, coral reefs, wetlands, estuaries, and alpine meadows) gives it greater ecological diversity than Norway. All three of these propositions are correct.

Step 3: Evaluation of the IUCN (2004) Described Species Count
According to the International Union for Conservation of Nature and Natural Resources (IUCN) (2004), the total number of plant and animal species described so far is slightly more than 1.5 million. The figure of about 7 million corresponds to Robert May's conservative estimate of total global species diversity (including undiscovered species). Therefore, attributing 7 million to IUCN (2004) as described species is incorrect.

Step 4: Evaluation of Insect Species Richness
Among recorded animal species, insects constitute the most species-rich taxonomic group, accounting for more than 70 per cent of the total (meaning 7 out of every 10 animals are insects). This proposition is correct.

Step 5: Final Conclusion
The propositions regarding Edward Wilson, amphibian species diversity in the Western Ghats, India's ecosystem diversity relative to Norway, and insects comprising over 70 per cent of animal species are correct, whereas the proposition stating that IUCN (2004) recorded over 7 million described species is incorrect.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER15_Q02 - Latitudinal gradients tropical productivity and species area equation

questiontext.text:
Consider the following five statements about patterns of biodiversity and identify the correct combination:

(I) With very few exceptions, the tropics (latitudinal range of \(23.5^{\circ}\text{ N}\) to \(23.5^{\circ}\text{ S}\)) harbour more species than temperate or polar areas.
(II) A forest in a tropical region like Ecuador has up to 10 times as many species of vascular plants as a forest of equal area in a temperate region like the Midwest of the USA.
(III) Tropical latitudes remained relatively undisturbed for millions of years unlike temperate regions subjected to frequent glaciations, providing a longer evolutionary time for species diversification.
(IV) Higher solar energy available in the tropics contributes to lower productivity, which indirectly limits species diversity.
(V) In the species-area relationship \(\log S = \log C + Z \log A\), \(Z\) is the slope of the line (regression coefficient), which lies in the range of 0.1 to 0.2 for smaller regions regardless of taxonomic group.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Species richness follows a pronounced latitudinal gradient peaking in the tropics due to evolutionary time, climatic stability, and solar energy, while within regions it increases with area according to a logarithmic linear relationship.

Step 2: Evaluation of Latitudinal Distribution and Vascular Plant Richness
With very few exceptions, tropical latitudes (\(23.5^{\circ}\text{ N}\) to \(23.5^{\circ}\text{ S}\)) support far more species than temperate or polar zones; for instance, a tropical forest in Ecuador contains up to 10 times as many vascular plant species as an equal-area temperate forest in the Midwest of the USA. Both propositions are correct.

Step 3: Evaluation of Evolutionary Time and Solar Productivity Hypotheses
Because tropical latitudes remained relatively undisturbed for millions of years without frequent glaciations, they had a longer evolutionary time for speciation. However, greater solar energy in the tropics contributes to higher productivity (not lower productivity), which in turn may contribute indirectly to greater species diversity. Thus, the evolutionary time proposition is correct, whereas the lower productivity proposition is incorrect.

Step 4: Evaluation of the Species-Area Regression Coefficient
In the logarithmic species-area equation \(\log S = \log C + Z \log A\), \(Z\) denotes the slope of the regression line. Across smaller regions and diverse taxonomic groups (such as plants in Britain, birds in California, or molluscs in New York state), ecologists found \(Z\) to lie consistently in the range of 0.1 to 0.2. This proposition is correct.

Step 5: Final Conclusion
The propositions on tropical species richness, Ecuador versus Midwest USA vascular plant diversity, undisturbed evolutionary time in the tropics, and the 0.1 to 0.2 range of \(Z\) for smaller regions are correct, while the proposition claiming lower tropical productivity is incorrect.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER15_Q03 - Tilman experiments Pacific Island extinctions and Sixth Extinction

questiontext.text:
Evaluate the following five statements regarding ecosystem functioning and biodiversity loss, and choose the correct option:

(I) In David Tilman's long-term outdoor plot experiments, plots with more species showed less year-to-year variation in total biomass and higher productivity.
(II) The colonisation of tropical Pacific Islands by humans is said to have led to the extinction of more than 2,000 species of native birds.
(III) Presently, 12 per cent of all bird species, 23 per cent of all mammal species, 32 per cent of all amphibian species, and 31 per cent of all gymnosperm species face the threat of extinction.
(IV) The last twenty years alone have witnessed the disappearance of 27 species, and more than 15,500 species worldwide currently face the threat of extinction.
(V) During the history of life on earth, there were five episodes of mass extinction, and the current 'Sixth Extinction' is occurring at a slower rate than those pre-human episodes.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Species richness promotes ecosystem stability and productivity, whereas human-driven extinctions are accelerating far beyond natural background and prehistoric mass extinction rates.

Step 2: Evaluation of Tilman's Experiments and Pacific Island Extinctions
David Tilman's long-term outdoor plot experiments showed that plots with higher species diversity exhibited less year-to-year variation in total biomass and higher overall productivity. Historically, human colonisation of tropical Pacific Islands led to the extinction of more than 2,000 native bird species. Both propositions are correct.

Step 3: Evaluation of Current Extinction Threats and Recent Disappearances
Currently, more than 15,500 species worldwide face extinction, including 12 per cent of all bird species, 23 per cent of all mammal species, 32 per cent of all amphibian species, and 31 per cent of all gymnosperm species; moreover, 27 species have disappeared in the last twenty years alone. Both propositions are correct.

Step 4: Evaluation of the Sixth Extinction Rate
Although fossil records show five earlier episodes of mass extinction over more than 3 billion years, the ongoing 'Sixth Extinction' differs sharply in rate: current species extinction rates are estimated to be 100 to 1,000 times faster than in pre-human times due to human activities, not slower. Thus, this proposition is incorrect.

Step 5: Final Conclusion
The propositions covering Tilman's plot experiments, Pacific Island bird extinctions, taxonomic threat percentages, and the 27 species lost in twenty years out of over 15,500 threatened species are correct, while the proposition claiming a slower Sixth Extinction rate is incorrect.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER15_Q04 - Evil Quartet habitat fragmentation invasive species and co extinction

questiontext.text:
Read the following five statements regarding 'The Evil Quartet' of biodiversity loss and select the option with only correct statements:

(I) Habitat loss and fragmentation is the most important cause driving animals and plants to extinction, badly affecting mammals and birds requiring large territories and animals with migratory habits.
(II) Over-harvesting of marine fish populations around the world is an example of over-exploitation that endangers commercially important species.
(III) Invasive weed species such as carrot grass (Parthenium), Lantana, and water hyacinth (Eichhornia) cause environmental damage and threaten native species.
(IV) The illegal introduction of the African catfish Clarias gariepinus for aquaculture purposes poses a threat to indigenous catfishes in Indian rivers.
(V) When a host fish species becomes extinct, its unique assemblage of parasites easily switches to unrelated terrestrial hosts without facing extinction.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The four major causes of biodiversity loss—habitat loss and fragmentation, over-exploitation, alien species invasions, and co-extinctions—drive rapid declines in native populations and dependent species.

Step 2: Evaluation of Habitat Fragmentation and Over-exploitation
Habitat loss and fragmentation is the primary driver of extinction; breaking large habitats into small fragments severely impacts mammals and birds needing large territories as well as migratory animals. Likewise, over-harvesting of marine fish populations exemplifies over-exploitation endangering commercially important species. Both propositions are correct.

Step 3: Evaluation of Invasive Alien Species in India
Alien species that become invasive threaten indigenous biodiversity. In India, invasive weeds like carrot grass (Parthenium), Lantana, and water hyacinth (Eichhornia) cause significant environmental damage, and the illegal introduction of the African catfish Clarias gariepinus for aquaculture threatens native riverine catfishes. Both propositions are correct.

Step 4: Evaluation of Co-extinction in Host-Parasite Pairs
Co-extinction occurs when species linked in an obligatory way perish together. When a host fish species becomes extinct, its unique assemblage of parasites also meets the same fate rather than switching to unrelated terrestrial hosts. Therefore, this proposition is incorrect.

Step 5: Final Conclusion
The propositions regarding habitat fragmentation, marine over-exploitation, invasive weeds, and the African catfish invasion are correct, whereas the proposition denying co-extinction of host-specific fish parasites is incorrect.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER15_Q05 - Conservation arguments hotspots protected areas and global summits

questiontext.text:
Consider the following five statements regarding why and how we conserve biodiversity, and identify the correct combination:

(I) More than 25 per cent of drugs currently sold worldwide are derived from plants, and 25,000 species of plants contribute to traditional medicines, supporting the narrowly utilitarian argument.
(II) The Amazon forest is estimated to produce, through photosynthesis, 20 per cent of the total oxygen in the earth's atmosphere, exemplifying the broadly utilitarian argument.
(III) The ethical argument for conserving biodiversity recognises that every species has an intrinsic value, even if it has no current economic value to humans.
(IV) Out of the 34 global biodiversity hotspots, three—Western Ghats and Sri Lanka, Indo-Burma, and Himalaya—cover India's exceptionally high biodiversity regions.
(V) India's in situ conservation network includes 14 biosphere reserves, 90 national parks, and 448 wildlife sanctuaries, while the 1992 Earth Summit was held in Johannesburg and the 2002 World Summit on Sustainable Development was held in Rio de Janeiro.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Biodiversity conservation rests on narrowly utilitarian, broadly utilitarian, and ethical arguments, and is executed through national protected-area networks, global hotspots, and international conventions.

Step 2: Evaluation of Conservation Arguments
Direct medicinal benefits (over 25 per cent of marketed drugs derived from plants and 25,000 plant species used in traditional medicine) support the narrowly utilitarian argument. Ecosystem services such as the Amazon forest producing 20 per cent of atmospheric oxygen via photosynthesis support the broadly utilitarian argument. The ethical argument affirms that every species possesses intrinsic value regardless of economic utility. All three propositions are correct.

Step 3: Evaluation of India's Biodiversity Hotspots
Among the 34 biodiversity hotspots identified globally, three—Western Ghats and Sri Lanka, Indo-Burma, and Himalaya—cover India's exceptionally rich biodiversity regions. This proposition is correct.

Step 4: Evaluation of Protected Areas and International Summits
India's legal in situ conservation framework includes 14 biosphere reserves, 90 national parks, and 448 wildlife sanctuaries. However, the historic Convention on Biological Diversity (The Earth Summit) in 1992 was held in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil, whereas the follow-up World Summit on Sustainable Development in 2002 was held in Johannesburg, South Africa. Swapping the host cities of the two summits makes this proposition incorrect.

Step 5: Final Conclusion
The propositions on narrowly utilitarian medicinal value, broadly utilitarian oxygen production by the Amazon, ethical intrinsic value, and the three Indian biodiversity hotspots are correct, while the proposition swapping the venues of the 1992 Earth Summit and the 2002 World Summit is incorrect.
